summary: 36b covers three topics: (1) R. Yehuda vs Rabbis on bull location is tied to nevelah liability in Temple precincts; (2) the full Yom Kippur confession formula - Anna HaShem, chatati, aviti, pashati, with the congregation responding Baruch Shem when the Divine Name is spoken; (3) v'chipper means kaparat devarim - verbal confession is the mechanism of atonement on Yom Kippur.

display.title: Why Does the Bull's Location Matter? Nevelah

learning.ahaMoment: The location of the confession is not merely spatial - it is tied to liability for nevelah in sacred spaces.
learning.memoryAnchor: Where the bull stands = where it might die = where nevelah might occur.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why would the exact spot where the High Priest's bull stands matter halachically, beyond ceremony?
learning.coreTension: R. Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree about where the bull stands for confession, and the Gemara asks whether this dispute is rooted in something more substantive than spatial preference.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara ties the location dispute to nevelah liability: if the bull were to die before slaughter while standing in one zone versus another, the Temple precincts impose different consequences, so the location choice carries real legal weight.

takeaway.text: A dispute that looks purely spatial (where the bull stands) is actually rooted in a substantive halachic concern: nevelah liability differs by zone within the Temple precincts.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners see the location dispute as a matter of staging or honor; it is in fact anchored in a deeper disagreement about sacred-zone liability for an animal that dies unslaughtered.

display.whats: The confession formula: 'I have sinned, transgressed, rebelled' - what order?
display.hint: 'Aviti, pashati, chatati' or 'chatati, aviti, pashati'? The halacha is stated.
display.title: The Full Confession Formula

learning.ahaMoment: The full confession formula names three categories of sin in a specific order, repeated twice - first admitting, then requesting atonement.
learning.memoryAnchor: Chatati, aviti, pashati: three sin-types, said twice - once admitting, once requesting forgiveness.
learning.learnerQuestion: What exact words does the High Priest say when he confesses over the bull?
learning.coreTension: Confession requires specific words, and a learner might assume a single general admission of guilt suffices rather than a structured formula.
learning.coreMove: The baraita gives the precise text: 'Anna HaShem, chatati, aviti, pashati' - naming three distinct categories of wrongdoing (sin, iniquity, rebellion), for himself, his household, and the priesthood, then repeating the same three categories in the request for atonement.

takeaway.text: The Yom Kippur confession is a fixed formula naming three distinct categories of wrongdoing, recited twice - once in admission and once in the plea for atonement - not a generic statement of guilt.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners assume any sincere admission of wrongdoing fulfills the confession requirement; the halacha fixes a specific three-part formula recited in a specific structure.

display.whats: 'V'chipper' (he shall atone) - what does 'atone' mean here? Atonement through words.
display.hint: Verbal confession (kaparat devarim) is the means of atonement for intentional sins.
display.title: Atonement Through Words

learning.ahaMoment: V'chipper = kaparat devarim: the confession speech itself is the atoning act, not just the sacrifice.
learning.memoryAnchor: Atonement is verbal: the blood atones for impurity, the words atone for sins.
learning.learnerQuestion: If the bull's blood already atones, why does the High Priest also need to say anything?
learning.coreTension: The verse states that the High Priest 'shall atone' (v'chipper), and the Gemara asks what kind of atoning act this word is describing, since the blood of the sacrifice already accomplishes a form of atonement.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara teaches that v'chipper refers specifically to kaparat devarim - atonement accomplished through speech - meaning the verbal confession itself is the atoning mechanism for deliberate sins, distinct from the blood's atonement for ritual impurity.

takeaway.text: Yom Kippur atonement operates on two distinct tracks: the sacrificial blood addresses ritual impurity, while the spoken confession (kaparat devarim) is the atoning act for deliberate sin.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners assume the blood sacrifice alone accomplishes atonement; the Gemara teaches that verbal confession is itself a required, independent atoning mechanism.

misconceptions.correction: The Gemara derives that v'chipper means kaparat devarim - the verbal confession is itself the atoning act for deliberate sins, distinct from and necessary alongside the blood's atonement for impurity.

rashiTranslations.en: They disagree about the prohibition of carrion - since it is written, a positive commandment follows it, 'to the convert who is within your gates
you shall give it, and he shall eat it' (Deuteronomy 14); but by necessity this is not converted to a positive commandment, since
giving it to the convert is impossible except after one has already transgressed the negative commandment against eating it, and by
necessity the positive commandment must mean from the outset: do not eat any carrion, but rather you shall give it to the convert
and not eat it yourself. Rabbi Akiva holds it is not
a proper prohibition - and one is lashed for it, and the prohibition of gleanings,
forgotten sheaves, and the corner is likewise a positive commandment that follows it
meant from the outset, and thus the verse states
(Leviticus 19), 'and the gleanings of your harvest you shall not gather;
rather, you shall leave it for the poor,' meaning do not gather it, and he is lashed
for it, and no burnt-offering comes for it. And Rabbi Yosei
HaGlili holds - the prohibition of carrion, even though
by necessity the positive commandment that follows it must mean from the outset,
since it is written right after the negative commandment,
one is not lashed for it, since it is not comparable to the prohibition against muzzling,
which does carry a burnt-offering; and the prohibition of gleanings, forgotten sheaves,
and the corner likewise, even if we say the positive commandment
that follows it means from the outset, still one is not
lashed for it. Abaye said: all agree about the prohibition of
carrion - since by necessity the positive commandment that follows it means from the outset
and it is a proper prohibition, and we lash for it.
But here, regarding 'leave' - the verse written after the prohibition of
gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner, they disagree. Rabbi
Yosei holds it means from now - after he has already gathered
and transgressed the negative commandment, the verse converted it
to a positive commandment and commanded him to leave it there for the poor and the convert,
and therefore he is not lashed for it. And Rabbi Akiva holds -
the positive commandment stands from the outset, before the gathering,
and he is lashed for it, since it is not converted to a positive commandment, and no burnt-offering
comes for it. And so regarding the scapegoat it
states - iniquities first, then transgressions,
and afterward sins. The rebels - one who acts
to provoke. The king of Moab rebelled against me - he rebelled
against me. Then Livnah rebelled - the residents of
Livnah rebelled against the king of Judah. He goes back and confesses
etc. - as a rhetorical question: if for the intentional sins he would already be forgiven
he would not need to ask again regarding the unintentional ones.
Treat their intentional sins as unintentional ones - and thus it means
'bearing iniquity and transgression' like an unwitting sin-offering. That
the verse supports him - meaning the Yom Kippur confession itself.
The one who went down before the ark - a prayer leader who arranges
in his own Yom Kippur prayer the order
of the High Priest's own services, based on
'so shall our lips substitute for bulls' (Hosea 14).
And he shall atone - what is stated regarding his own bull, 'and he shall atone for himself
and for his household' (Leviticus 16), refers to words of confession.
It is stated below regarding the scapegoat, 'he shall stand
alive before the Lord to atone for him' (ibid). And if
you wish to say - to answer a rebuttal to
this gezeirah shavah, saying that 'and he shall atone' means only
through the presentation of the blood, by necessity from that very verse itself
you can derive that it is impossible to say so,
since it states, 'and Aaron shall present
the bull of the sin-offering that is his, and he shall atone for himself
and for his household,' and only afterward, 'and he shall slaughter
the bull of the sin-offering,' etc. By necessity, 'and he shall atone
for himself' is said while it has still not been slaughtered; so it emerges that
this atonement is through words. What does 'and if you wish to say' mean - what
response did he need to give, that another reason was required? And if you would say,
let us derive it - that this 'and he shall atone' comes from the atonement written regarding the inner goat, where it is written,

'and he shall atone for the Sanctuary from the impurities of the children of Israel' - but that one is through the presentation of blood, since it is written after the presentation of the blood, and moreover it has no confession.
And from where - the daf ends mid-comment here; the comment (deriving the confession's own opening word from a shared verbal analogy) continues on 37a.
